intro_band.agent_remit_summary: yaah is a local, single-developer command-line tool that generates coding-agent configuration for four agents — Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex CLI, and GitHub Copilot CLI — from one Go source of truth, and ships a uniform protective toolset alongside every configuration: five event hooks (a linter, a catastrophic-command guard, a secret scanner, a comment/placeholder checker, and a session logger), a built-in check-only MCP server (`yaah serve`), and a durable per-session audit log under `.claude/sessions/`. It performs no LLM inference of its own. Its central promise is that these protections are delivered uniformly across every generated agent, that catastrophic shell commands MUST be blocked before execution, that hardcoded credentials MUST be caught before an edit is accepted, and that third-party MCP servers and remote skills MUST be reached over TLS at pinned, integrity-checked versions.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: A Go 1.25 CLI (cobra) organised as an Interface -> Registry -> Generator architecture under `pkg/`, with the harness in `pkg/harness/harness.go` wiring hook, MCP, LSP, skill, agent, command and plugin registries. The five protective hooks live in `pkg/hooks/handlers/` and run as Claude Code hook commands (`yaah hook <event>`), which exit code 2 to block; `HandleHookEvent` records tool calls, blocked calls and file modifications to a JSON session store in `pkg/session/store.go`. `pkg/mcpserver/` exposes seven MCP tools over stdio (six check-only plus one workspace-writing `yaah_planning_init`). Per-agent output is produced by four generators in `pkg/generator/`; `hookmap.go` maps Claude hook events to each target, and remote skills/agents are fetched by `pkg/gitcache/` at pinned commit SHAs. The materially divergent surface is the Codex generator, whose emitted hook set omits the PreToolUse and PostToolUse events entirely.

behavior_summary: yaah is a genuinely security-oriented harness whose controls are real and enforcing on its primary target — the command guard blocks catastrophic shell commands before execution, the secret scanner blocks credential-bearing edits, and a structured JSON session store durably records tool calls and blocked commands — yet those protections are not delivered uniformly across the four agents it configures. The dominant pattern is a uniformity gap: the generated Codex configuration ships without the enforcing PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks (`hookmap.go` has no Codex mapping for either), so the command guard and secret scanner degrade to advisory `yaah` MCP check-tools the model may simply never call, and Codex sessions capture no tool-call audit trail. A second, cross-cutting theme is that the control layer is itself unverified and its trust boundaries partly under-pinned: the five protective handlers have no tests at all, there is no threat model or security-disclosure process, and while Go dependencies and remote skills are pinned, the `context7` and `notion` MCP servers are fetched unpinned via `npx -y` on every run.

rules.rule_text: Operating as a hosted, networked, or multi-tenant service — yaah is a local single-developer CLI.
Performing LLM inference of its own, or acting as an autonomous agent without a supervising developer at the terminal.
Weakening or removing the protective hooks from a generated configuration so that an agent ships without the full protection set.
Fetching yaah itself and third-party MCP server packages; MUST resolve pinned, integrity-checked versions.
Any counterparty reached without TLS when the connection is remote.
yaah_planning_init — the one built-in MCP tool that writes to the workspace; workspace writes require the developer's review.
Hardcoded credentials MUST be detected before an edit that introduces them is accepted; they MUST NOT be written into committed files unremarked.
Agent-managed, session-loaded files MUST NOT be writable in a way that lets content the agent ingested from an untrusted source persist into future sessions unreviewed.
Repository contents, edited-file contents, and session audit logs MUST NOT leave the local workspace for any destination other than the authorized counterparties above.
High-impact actions — destructive shell commands, file writes, and MCP tools that write, send, or execute — MUST reach a human checkpoint before they run.

Catastrophic shell commands — recursive deletion from the filesystem root, force-pushing to a main branch, hard resets, destructive database statements, filesystem formatting, raw disk writes — MUST be blocked before they execute.
Any generated agent configuration that ships WITHOUT the full protective hook set (linter, command guard, secret scanner, comment checker, session logger) that the harness promises.

MCP tool descriptions — the built-in server's, and, as far as the harness can inspect them, those of the third-party servers it configures — MUST NOT contain instruction-like language directed at the model (tool-poisoning indicator).
Third-party MCP servers MUST be pinned to a known-good, integrity-checked version — no server package auto-installed afresh, unpinned, on every run.
Dependencies MUST be version-controlled with a committed, pinned lockfile, and the dependency tree kept small and reviewable.
The MCP server configuration and the per-agent configuration files stay consistent with each other — a change to one MUST NOT silently leave the other stale.

The project publishes a threat model and a security-disclosure process, and its own protections are adversarially tested — confirming the secret scanner catches a planted secret, the command guard blocks a catastrophic command, a poisoning write into a session-loaded file is prevented, and a generated configuration genuinely carries the protections it claims.
a shell command the command guard has blocked MUST NOT be re-attempted or auto-approved on retry.
Every hook event — tool calls, blocked commands, file modifications, and security findings — is recorded to the durable per-session audit log, whether or not it also raised an alert.

rules.section: Escalation Rules — Alert Operator (Do Not Halt)
rules.rule_text: The secret scanner detects a hardcoded credential in an edited file — the edit is blocked and the finding surfaced to the developer.

findings.summary: Generated Codex configuration omits the enforcing PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks, so the command guard and secret scanner are not delivered as hooks for Codex.
findings.description: The cross-agent hook map has no Codex entry for PreToolUse or PostToolUse, so the Codex generator emits a hooks.json containing only SessionStart and Stop — the command guard, secret scanner, linter and comment checker never run on Codex tool activity. The yaah MCP server is wired into config.toml, but its check-only tools are advisory (the model may never call them) rather than a blocking gate, and no Pre/PostToolUse hook fires so Codex sessions record no tool-call audit. This partially satisfies the remit's own MCP-delivery escape hatch but degrades the protections from enforcing to optional, violating the "no generated agent runs without them" intent.
policy_rule_text: Weakening or removing the protective hooks from a generated configuration so that an agent ships without the full protection set.
Any generated agent configuration that ships WITHOUT the full protective hook set (linter, command guard, secret scanner, comment checker, session logger) that the harness promises.

evidence.snippet: hookMappings has no Codex value for HookPreToolUse (line 30) or HookPostToolUse (line 35) — only SessionStart, Stop and notify map to Codex.
GenerateHooks skips any event whose CodexEventName is empty, so the emitted .codex/hooks.json carries only SessionStart+Stop — no command-guard or secret-scanner hook.

recommended_actions: Deliver the PreToolUse command guard and PostToolUse secret/lint/comment checks to Codex — either by mapping Codex's available tool-call hook events in hookmap.go, or by making the yaah MCP check-tools a mandatory pre-execution step rather than advisory.
Ensure Codex sessions produce a tool-call audit trail equivalent to the Claude path so blocked commands and file modifications are recorded.

findings.summary: Third-party MCP servers context7 and notion are fetched unpinned via `npx -y` on every run, with no version pin or integrity check.
findings.description: The context7 provider launches `npx -y @context7/mcp` and the notion provider launches `npx -y @notionhq/notion-mcp-server`, both of which resolve and install the latest published package fresh on every invocation. This is the exact "server package auto-installed afresh, unpinned, on every run" pattern the remit forbids and directly contradicts the harness's otherwise-strong pinning discipline for Go dependencies and remote skills. A malicious or compromised upstream release would be pulled silently into the developer's session.
policy_rule_text: Fetching yaah itself and third-party MCP server packages; MUST resolve pinned, integrity-checked versions.
Third-party MCP servers MUST be pinned to a known-good, integrity-checked version — no server package auto-installed afresh, unpinned, on every run.

evidence.snippet: Args []string{"-y", "@context7/mcp"} with Command "npx" — no version pin, resolves latest on each launch.
context7 configured as npx -y @context7/mcp in the generated project MCP config, matching the provider default.

recommended_actions: Pin context7 and notion (and any npx-launched MCP server) to an exact published version, e.g. `@context7/mcp@<version>`, and prefer an integrity-checked install path over `npx -y`.
Extend the supply-chain baseline check (doctor) to flag any MCP server launched via an unpinned package specifier.

findings.summary: The command guard blocks only seven fixed regex patterns and misses long-form flag variants and many catastrophic commands.
findings.description: The default blocklist catches `rm -rf /`, a force-push to main/master, `git reset --hard`, `DROP TABLE/DATABASE`, `mkfs.`, and `dd of=/dev/`, but the patterns are literal enough to bypass — `rm --recursive --force /`, `rm -fr /`, `git push -f`, `TRUNCATE`/`DELETE FROM`, `chmod -R 777 /`, a shell fork bomb, and `curl ... | sh` all pass. The remit explicitly flags long-form flag coverage as a risk sensitivity, so this is a real gap in an otherwise operative control (the guard does block before execution on Claude, Copilot and OpenCode).
policy_rule_text: Catastrophic shell commands — recursive deletion from the filesystem root, force-pushing to a main branch, hard resets, destructive database statements, filesystem formatting, raw disk writes — MUST be blocked before they execute.

evidence.snippet: NewCommandGuard registers exactly 7 literal regexes (rm -rf /, git push --force main|master, git reset --hard, DROP TABLE|DATABASE, :>/ , mkfs., dd of=/dev/) — no coverage for long-form flags or equivalent destructive commands.

recommended_actions: Broaden the guard to normalise commands and match flag variants (e.g. `--recursive --force`, `-fr`, `git push -f`, `--force-with-lease`), and add patterns for chmod -R on root, fork bombs, and piped remote execution.
Add adversarial tests asserting each catastrophic-command variant is blocked (see PRAX-2026-07-27-008).

findings.summary: The secret scanner runs as a PostToolUse hook, so credentials are detected only after the edit has already been written to disk, and via a narrow 13-pattern denylist.
findings.description: The remit requires hardcoded credentials to be detected before an edit that introduces them is accepted, but the scanner fires on PostToolUse — by the time it blocks (exit 2, fed back to the model), the credential is already on disk and could already be staged or committed. The 13 regex patterns also cover a fixed set (AWS, GitHub, OpenAI, Anthropic, Slack, SendGrid, private keys, generic 8+ char password/secret) and miss classes such as GCP service-account keys, Azure keys, and generic high-entropy tokens.
policy_rule_text: Hardcoded credentials MUST be detected before an edit that introduces them is accepted; they MUST NOT be written into committed files unremarked.
The secret scanner detects a hardcoded credential in an edited file — the edit is blocked and the finding surfaced to the developer.

evidence.snippet: Events() returns HookPostToolUse only — the scan runs after the Edit/Write tool has applied the change, so the file already contains the secret when detection occurs.
NewSecretScanner registers 13 fixed provider-specific patterns; no GCP/Azure key or generic high-entropy detection.

recommended_actions: Move credential detection to a PreToolUse (pre-write) gate or scan the pending tool_input content so a secret-bearing edit is rejected before it lands on disk.
Broaden the pattern set and consider an entropy-based check to catch credential classes the fixed denylist omits.

findings.summary: The workspace-writing MCP tool yaah_planning_init executes on call with no in-harness approval checkpoint, though the remit designates it approval-required.
findings.description: The remit lists yaah_planning_init as a restricted tool whose workspace writes require the developer's review, and states that MCP tools which write MUST reach a human checkpoint before running. The yaah MCP server registers and executes it directly with no gating — a model call creates the .planning directory tree and STATE.md immediately. The blast radius is bounded (it only scaffolds a fixed directory set and refuses if .planning already exists), so this is a Medium rather than a high-impact write, but the stated approval requirement is unmet in yaah's own runtime.
policy_rule_text: yaah_planning_init — the one built-in MCP tool that writes to the workspace; workspace writes require the developer's review.
High-impact actions — destructive shell commands, file writes, and MCP tools that write, send, or execute — MUST reach a human checkpoint before they run.

evidence.snippet: addPlanningInitTool's handler calls os.MkdirAll and os.WriteFile to create .planning and STATE.md with no approval or confirmation step before the write.

recommended_actions: Gate yaah_planning_init behind an explicit confirmation or a dry-run/confirm two-step in the MCP server, or document that it relies on the host client's per-tool approval and enforce that assumption.

findings.summary: The structured session audit records tool calls, blocked calls and file changes but never populates the security-findings channel, and a redundant plaintext lifecycle log runs in parallel.
findings.description: The remit promises the per-session audit log captures security findings alongside tool calls, blocked commands and file modifications, and the Session struct has a dedicated Findings array — but HandleHookEvent never writes to it, so secret/lint/comment findings are persisted only indirectly when a handler blocks (captured as a BlockedCall reason); non-blocking findings such as lint formatting output reach stdout only. Separately, the SessionLogger handler writes a second, free-form plaintext log to .claude/logs/sessions.log that records session lifecycle events only, duplicating and diverging from the structured store under .claude/sessions/.
policy_rule_text: Every hook event — tool calls, blocked commands, file modifications, and security findings — is recorded to the durable per-session audit log, whether or not it also raised an alert.

evidence.snippet: The session-update block records ToolCalls, BlockedCalls and FilesModified but makes no assignment to sess.Findings — the Finding channel is dead.
SessionLogger writes plaintext "[ts] event=... session=... cwd=..." lines to .claude/logs/sessions.log, a lifecycle-only log separate from the structured .claude/sessions store.

recommended_actions: Populate Session.Findings from handler results (secret, lint, comment) in HandleHookEvent so all security findings — not only blocking ones — are durably recorded.
Consolidate the plaintext lifecycle log into the structured session store, or document why both exist, to avoid a divergent audit trail.

findings.summary: Generated session-loaded files (AGENTS.md, skills, agents) are written world-readable with no immutability or write-review control, leaving a memory-poisoning persistence surface.
findings.description: The remit forbids agent-managed, session-loaded files from being writable in a way that lets content ingested from an untrusted source persist into future sessions unreviewed, and flags their writability as a memory-poisoning risk. yaah writes the generated skills, agents and command files (which Claude Code re-loads into context each session) as ordinary 0644 files and ships no control that makes them read-only or reviews edits to them — the secret and comment hooks catch secrets and placeholders but not arbitrary poisoned prose. This is a structural ASI06 surface; no confirmed injection path within yaah itself elevates it beyond Medium.
policy_rule_text: Agent-managed, session-loaded files MUST NOT be writable in a way that lets content the agent ingested from an untrusted source persist into future sessions unreviewed.

evidence.snippet: WriteAllForTarget writes generated skill/agent/command files with os.WriteFile(..., 0o644) and no mechanism to mark session-loaded files read-only or to review later edits to them.

recommended_actions: Add an integrity/review control for session-loaded generated files — e.g. record a checksum manifest and have a hook warn when a generated AGENTS.md/skill/agent is modified out of band before it re-enters context.

findings.summary: The five protective hook handlers have no tests, and the project ships no threat model or security-disclosure process, contradicting the remit's adversarial-testing expectation.
findings.description: The remit expects the harness's own protections to be adversarially tested — confirming the secret scanner catches a planted secret, the command guard blocks a catastrophic command, a session-file poisoning write is prevented, and a generated configuration genuinely carries its protections — and that a threat model and disclosure process are published. In fact the pkg/hooks/handlers/ package has no test files at all (tests exist only for generators, catalog, gitcache and remote loaders), so the security-critical regex denylists are entirely unverified, and there is no SECURITY.md, threat model, or disclosure process anywhere in the repository.
policy_rule_text: The project publishes a threat model and a security-disclosure process, and its own protections are adversarially tested — confirming the secret scanner catches a planted secret, the command guard blocks a catastrophic command, a poisoning write into a session-loaded file is prevented, and a generated configuration genuinely carries the protections it claims.

evidence.snippet: Directory contains guard.go, secretscan.go, linter.go, commentcheck.go, sessionlog.go but no *_test.go — the protective controls are untested.
Repository has docs/components.md and docs/configuration.md but no SECURITY.md, threat model, or security-disclosure process.

recommended_actions: Add adversarial unit tests for each protective handler asserting planted secrets are caught, catastrophic-command variants are blocked, and every generated target carries the full protection set.
Publish a threat model and a SECURITY.md security-disclosure process.

positives.title: Enforcing command guard blocks catastrophic shell commands
positives.description: CommandGuard runs as a PreToolUse hook and `yaah hook` exits code 2 on a match, so blocked catastrophic commands are genuinely prevented before execution on Claude Code, Copilot and OpenCode targets.

positives.title: Durable structured per-session audit store
positives.description: HandleHookEvent records tool calls, blocked calls with reasons, and file modifications to a per-session JSON file with atomic temp-then-rename writes, and session IDs are validated against path traversal.

positives.title: Remote skills and agents pinned to commit SHAs
positives.description: Every remote skill and agent is loaded via `uses` references pinned to 40-character commit SHAs and fetched by gitcache, giving integrity-checked, reproducible remote content.

positives.title: Pinned, minimal Go dependency tree with signed releases
positives.description: go.mod/go.sum pin all two direct and eight indirect dependencies with committed hashes, CI actions are pinned to full SHAs, and GoReleaser signs release checksums with cosign and emits SBOMs.

positives.title: Experimental fact-checker correctly gated off by default
positives.description: The experimental Stop/SubagentStop fact-check hooks are installed only when the `YAAH_EXPERIMENTAL_FACT_CHECK` environment variable is set, matching the remit's approval-required posture.

rows.purpose: durable audit of tool calls, blocked calls with reasons, files modified, timestamps and event counts
session lifecycle events (start/end/stop) with session ID and cwd only

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Partial. yaah has real, operative Zero-Trust and monitoring controls — an enforcing command guard, a blocking secret scanner, and a durable structured session audit log — placing it above a hobby project, but coverage is incomplete in ways that keep it out of the Established band overall. Its strongest dimension is supply chain: pinned Go dependencies, SHA-pinned remote skills, cosign-signed releases with SBOMs, and SHA-pinned CI actions, marred only by unpinned `npx` MCP servers. Its weakest is Build an AI Red Team: the security-critical hook handlers carry no tests and the project ships no threat model or adversarial-testing evidence, despite the remit expecting exactly that. The double-weighted Zero-Trust score is held to Partial by the Codex uniformity gap, a narrow command-guard denylist, and post-write secret detection.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: yaah performs no inference and its own capability surface is tightly bounded — seven MCP tools (six check-only, one bounded scaffold write) and five hooks, matching the Known Good Baseline — so the domain is clearly limited; the only breadth concern is that `AllDefaults` in `pkg/harness/defaults.go` enables a large roster of remote skills, agents and plugins by default.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: Remote skill and agent content is fetched at pinned commit SHAs via `pkg/gitcache`, and yaah ingests no untrusted external content into any LLM context of its own; the residual gap is that generated session-loaded files (AGENTS.md, skills, agents) are written world-writable with no review or immutability control, leaving an ASI06 persistence surface.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: The command guard is a real PreToolUse block (exit 2) and the secret scanner blocks credential-bearing edits, but enforcement is Partial — the Codex configuration omits the enforcing pre/post hooks entirely, the command-guard denylist is only seven regex patterns that miss long-form flag variants, the secret scanner fires post-write, and the one workspace-writing MCP tool (`yaah_planning_init`) has no approval gate.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: Go dependencies are exact-pinned with a committed `go.sum` and a minimal tree, remote skills/agents are pinned to 40-character commit SHAs, CI actions are pinned to full SHAs, and releases are cosign-signed with SBOMs; the one clear divergence is `context7` and `notion` MCP servers fetched unpinned via `npx -y @.../mcp` on every run, violating the remit's MCP-pinning MUST.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: A test suite exists but covers only generators, catalog, gitcache and remote loaders — the five security-critical hook handlers in `pkg/hooks/handlers/` have no tests at all, and there is no threat model, security-disclosure process, or adversarial-testing evidence, despite the remit explicitly expecting the protections to be adversarially tested.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: `HandleHookEvent` in `pkg/harness/harness.go` writes a durable, structured, timestamped JSON audit of tool calls, blocked calls with reasons, and file modifications to `.claude/sessions/<id>.json`, with `session list/show/clean` tooling; the gaps are that the `Session.Findings` channel is never populated, non-blocking findings are not persisted, and Codex sessions record no tool calls because no pre/post hook fires.
